faq.answer: No score on this facet establishes social anxiety. Wanting less group contact and feeling fearful or distressed about contact are different questions, and they can coexist. If persistent distress interferes with the contact you want or with daily life, seek assessment from a qualified professional rather than treating a personality label as the explanation.
faq.question: Does lower Gregariousness mean social anxiety?

faq.answer: Yes. A preference for group company does not prevent satisfying time alone. Different activities, recovery needs, and relationships can make both arrangements appealing.
faq.question: Can I enjoy solitude and still prefer groups?

faq.answer: Your skills may exceed the amount of interaction you want. The particular event, recent social workload, or practical demands may also explain your reluctance. Look for recurring choices under comparable conditions rather than drawing a conclusion from one invitation.
faq.question: Why am I good with people but reluctant to attend?

faq.answer: Not by itself. You may be missing a particular relationship, suitable contact, or a sense of belonging. Ask what kind of contact you want; loneliness does not specify a preferred group size.
faq.question: Is loneliness evidence of high Gregariousness?

faq.answer: It can be a useful clue about that setting. Work obligations, shared interests, and the difference between text and live interaction also matter. Describe the format instead of assuming that online frequency predicts all group preferences.
faq.question: Does frequent online participation count?

faq.answer: They can show that those gatherings suited you under those conditions. A short planned trial cannot establish lasting trait change. Keep it separate from spontaneous choices and use the experience to decide which arrangements to repeat.
faq.question: Can a few planned gatherings show that I have changed?

not_for: Do not use this page for clinical diagnosis or as the sole basis for hiring or admission.
method_boundary.summary: Use this page to understand personality concepts and examine everyday behavior. Interpret actual scores using the instrument’s scoring method, reference sample, and intended use.

sections.body:
Gregariousness describes the appeal of being with groups and participating in group interaction. In the NEO/IPIP-NEO vocabulary used here, it is a facet of [Extraversion](/en/personality/big-five/extraversion).

A useful question is what you would choose when the activity is suitable and attendance is feasible. Would you rather join several people, arrange a smaller interaction, or spend the time by yourself? A stronger tendency can make group company more appealing; a weaker tendency can make less crowded arrangements preferable. A middle position can include both choices or different preferences in different settings. These are positions on a continuum, not separate personality types.

Your actual attendance is a mixture of preference and circumstances. Invitations, caring responsibilities, transport, cost, accessibility, and work can determine who gets to attend. Count choices only after considering those conditions.
sections.heading: Start with preference, not attendance

sections.body:
Being good at conversation does not tell you how often someone wants group interaction. A person may handle a community event competently and choose a quiet weekend afterwards. Another may eagerly attend but have difficulty noticing when someone else wants a turn to speak. Interaction skills need their own evidence.

[Warmth](/en/personality/big-five/facets/warmth) concerns friendly connection with people. Group preference concerns the arrangement of company. Neither the size of a gathering nor how often you attend tells us how considerate you are toward a particular person.

Loneliness is also a separate question: does your current contact meet what you want from relationships? Limited group contact can be satisfying or unwanted. Frequent contact can also leave someone wanting closer connection. Do not use a crowded calendar as proof that relationships are fulfilling.

Enjoying a group need not mean enjoying every kind of stimulation. A familiar discussion group and a noisy public celebration differ in more than headcount. [Excitement Seeking](/en/personality/big-five/facets/excitement-seeking) helps distinguish attraction to stimulation from attraction to company.
sections.heading: Company, connection, skill, and loneliness

sections.body:
Useful clues include whether you voluntarily join an available group activity, want to continue after the planned activity ends, or invite others into something you could do alone. Record how appealing the option felt as well as what you did.

Mandatory attendance provides different information. Staying for a work event may reflect responsibility. Leaving promptly may reflect a train departure. Being quiet in a group may reflect difficulty hearing, unfamiliar language, or a preference to listen. None of those observations establishes how much company the person wanted.

Keep online settings specific too. An ongoing text conversation, a live video group, and a room full of people offer different experiences. Preference in one setting is not automatically preference in all of them.
sections.heading: Look for choices you could actually make

sections.body:
Consider this illustrative situation. A resident often joins the shared sessions at a community garden and continues chatting while tools are put away. They initially describe themselves as someone who always prefers company.

On a day when several neighbours are available, they freely choose to work alone on a planting plan. They enjoy that afternoon as well. This naturally occurring exception makes 'always' inaccurate. Looking more closely, they like group company during practical shared work but often prefer solitude when deciding what to plant.

An earlier missed session is different: they were caring for a relative and could not attend. It tells us about availability. A later session they deliberately attend to compare experiences is different again: it is a planned trial. Keeping these events distinct prevents a attendance count from becoming a personality verdict.
sections.heading: A natural exception can improve the description

sections.body:
If you often add group plans, check whether the schedule still makes room for recovery, responsibilities, and the individual relationships you value. Enjoying company does not guarantee endless stamina or make time alone unnecessary.

If you usually limit group contact, ask whether that amount is satisfying. There is no requirement to match another person's calendar. If you want more connection, the obstacle may be finding an appealing format rather than becoming a different kind of person. A recurring activity with a manageable group may be worth considering.

With friends or colleagues, describe the conditions you need: the activity, approximate group size, duration, and time to yourself afterwards. Those details are easier to negotiate than a judgment about who is sociable enough. Less group contact does not guarantee greater depth or independence, and more contact does not guarantee a reliable support network.
sections.heading: Use the distinction to make better arrangements

sections.body:
Choose a narrow question, such as 'Do I usually want to join familiar group activities when I have free time?' For the next few naturally occurring options, note who was involved, the activity, whether attendance was feasible, what you initially wanted, what you chose, and how the experience felt.

Separate an available option you declined from an option you could not take. For a declined option, record the reason rather than assuming it was preference. If you find no exception to your initial impression, check whether a meaningful alternative ever appeared. Not finding a counterexample is weaker evidence than having a suitable opportunity and choosing differently.

After observing, you can try one voluntary arrangement with an easy exit: a brief familiar group activity, or some quiet time within an otherwise social schedule. Write down your expectation beforehand. Afterwards, ask whether you would repeat it and which conditions mattered. Label this as a deliberate trial rather than ordinary behaviour.

Retain a provisional description if similar feasible choices repeatedly fit it. Narrow it if the appeal depends on shared interests or familiar people. Set it aside if opportunities are scarce or recent exhaustion dominates the observations. This process helps plan contact; it does not validate a trait or show that a short exercise changed your personality.
sections.heading: Observe ordinary choices before trying a change

sections.body:
The [official IPIP comparison table](https://ipip.ori.org/newNEO_FacetsTable.htm) links Gregariousness to the corresponding NEO facet. The [longer IPIP item set](https://ipip.ori.org/newNEOFacetsKey.htm) includes group participation and solitude preferences. The [Maples four-item version](https://ipip.ori.org/30FacetNEO-PI-RItems_Maples_etal.htm) samples a narrower set of situations.

These are descriptions of related constructs and particular instruments. They do not make scores from different measures or translations interchangeable. This guide does not establish which facets a particular FermatMind questionnaire measures. If your result reports only a broad domain, use the facet as a question for reflection rather than inventing an additional measured score.
sections.heading: What the sources establish

sections.body:
Read [Extraversion](/en/personality/big-five/extraversion) for the broader domain, [Warmth](/en/personality/big-five/facets/warmth) for friendly connection, and [Assertiveness](/en/personality/big-five/facets/assertiveness) for stepping forward and directing a discussion.

For the pace of activity, see [Activity](/en/personality/big-five/facets/activity). For stimulation and pleasant emotion, see [Excitement Seeking](/en/personality/big-five/facets/excitement-seeking) and [Positive Emotions](/en/personality/big-five/facets/positive-emotions). The [facet guide](/en/personality/big-five/facets) explains how these terms fit together.
